issues.legal_issue: Tenancy rights that were consistently treated as jointly held could not be transferred exclusively to one heir on the basis of a convenience consent, and transactions dependent on that transfer were invalid.
material_facts: After the original tenant died, his widow and sons were treated by the municipal landlord and by the family as joint tenants, including in earlier eviction proceedings that ended in an unchallenged finding that the heirs were tenants.
A consent letter was issued while the joint tenants faced eviction, but the widow later asked only for rent receipts to be transferred to one son and stated that the tenancy was joint.

The heirs later asserted joint tenancy in court proceedings, and a written objection to an exclusive transfer was received by the municipal landlord before it purported to transfer the tenancy to one heir.
The widow's unprobated will bequeathed the nursery business, not the tenancy; the record showed no relinquishment of the other heirs' tenancy rights.
The municipal landlord transferred the tenancy exclusively to one heir, who later surrendered part of it in exchange for a new lease and constructed a building on the leased plot.
issues.conclusion: The tenancy remained jointly held by the heirs. The exclusive transfer to one heir was illegal and void, and the subsequent surrender, replacement lease, and construction founded on that transfer were also void or illegal.
issues.legal_principle: Tenancy succession is generally governed by the applicable statute; absent a provision to the contrary, ordinary succession applies. Gian Devi Anand v. Jeevan Kumar (1985) and State of West Bengal v. Kailash Chandra Kapur (1997) support heritability or testamentary disposition where no contrary restriction applies. The Court also considered Bhavarlal Labhchand Shah v. Kanaiyalal Nathalal Intawala (1986), Vasant Pratap Pandit v. Dr. Anant Trimbak Sabnis (1994), Sangappa Kalyanappa Bangi v. Land Tribunal (1998), H.C. Pandey v. G.C. Paul (1989), and Parvinder Singh v. Renu Gautam (2004) on tenancy succession and testamentary transfer. Here, the Bombay Rent Control Act, 1947 excluded this tenancy under Section 4(1), and the municipal statute was silent. The Court relied on Section 213 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925, under which a legatee under an unprobated Parsi will could not claim the bequest, and Section 52 as it stood before its 1991 amendment, under which a Parsi female intestate's property passed equally to her children. The parties' repeated treatment of the tenancy as joint, the earlier unchallenged judicial finding, the limited purpose and later withdrawal of the consent, and the absence of a valid testamentary transfer of the tenancy established that no exclusive transfer or relinquishment occurred.

rule.if: civil_tenancy_dispute and original_tenant_left_multiple_heirs and heirs_and_landlord_treated_tenancy_as_joint and testamentary_document_did_not_transfer_tenancy and consent_was_limited_to_convenience_or_rent_records and consent_was_later_withdrawn

predicates.civil_tenancy_dispute: The proceeding concerned the succession to and transfer of tenancy rights after a tenant's death.
predicates.original_tenant_left_multiple_heirs: The original tenant died leaving more than one heir with a potential claim to the tenancy.
predicates.heirs_and_landlord_treated_tenancy_as_jo: The heirs and the landlord repeatedly treated the heirs as joint tenants, including in earlier proceedings.
predicates.testamentary_document_did_not_transfer_t: The testamentary document relied on did not validly bequeath the tenancy rights to one heir.
predicates.consent_was_limited_to_convenience_or_re: The consent relied on for an exclusive transfer was given for convenience or for changing rent records, rather than to relinquish the other heirs' rights.
predicates.consent_was_later_withdrawn: The other heirs later withdrew or contradicted the consent before the landlord acted on it.

issues.definition: When a tenancy dispute involves multiple heirs whom the heirs and landlord treated as joint tenants, and the asserted testamentary transfer and consent did not validly give one heir the exclusive tenancy, the exclusive transfer and transactions dependent on it are invalid.

issues.legal_issue: An appellate court may account for material subsequent events when deciding whether the relief claimed has become inappropriate, and may mould relief to achieve complete justice while respecting procedural fairness.
material_facts: During the suits, an interim order permitted construction on the condition that five flats be kept reserved subject to the outcome of the litigation.
A later interim order continued the restriction against creating third-party rights in the reserved flats.
The appellants proceeded with construction knowing that the rights to the reserved flats remained subject to the litigation, and obtained benefits from other flats in the building.

By the time of the appeals, the tenancy transfer and the replacement lease on which the construction depended had been held invalid, and the municipal landlord had acquired the remaining portions of the property.
The respondents claimed a 6/15 share; the High Court allocated the reserved flats to them, and the Supreme Court found no specific contrary submission undermining that share determination.
issues.conclusion: The High Court acted within its appellate powers in considering the subsequent events and moulding the relief; the allocation of the five reserved flats to the respondents as representing their share was upheld.
issues.legal_principle: Although rights are ordinarily assessed as at the institution of the suit, a court may take cautious cognizance of subsequent events that materially affect entitlement to relief or the way relief should be moulded, provided fairness to both sides is maintained. Relief may be moulded where subsequent events make the original relief inappropriate, taking account of the changes would shorten litigation or enable complete justice, and the events are brought to the court's attention promptly and in accordance with procedural rules. The Court relied on Pasupuleti Venkateswarlu v. The Motor and General Traders (1975), Ramesh Kumar v. Kesho Ram (1992), Om Prakash Gupta as discussed in Sheshambal v. Chelur Corporation (2010), and Lachmeshwar Prasad Shukul v. Keshwar Lal Choudhury (1941), among other authorities. Section 96 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 did not prevent the High Court from moulding relief on that basis.

rule.if: first_appeal_in_civil_suit and subsequent_events_materially_changed_the_relief_context and subsequent_events_were_brought_to_the_court_attention and affected_parties_had_fair_opportunity and interim_construction_was_conditional_on_reserved_flats

predicates.first_appeal_in_civil_suit: The proceeding was a first appeal arising from civil suits.
predicates.subsequent_events_materially_changed_the: Events after the suits began materially changed what relief would be appropriate or effective.
predicates.subsequent_events_were_brought_to_the_co: The changed circumstances were placed before the court while the litigation was pending.
predicates.affected_parties_had_fair_opportunity: The parties affected by the proposed relief had a fair opportunity to address the relevant circumstances.
predicates.interim_construction_was_conditional_on_: Construction was allowed during the litigation on condition that specified flats remain reserved subject to its outcome.

issues.definition: When a civil first appeal presents material subsequent events fairly brought to the court's attention and construction proceeded subject to reserved flats, the appellate court may mould relief by awarding those flats to the claimants as equitable relief.
